--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate it. Uh quick intro, I'm Maya, AE on the account, with Ethan and Priya from our SE team. Luis: you wanna kick off with context?
[00:12] Luis: Sure thanks Maya. We're looking to pilot an assistant for retail banking — high volume, sensitive PII, and we need to decide whether to start on Hosted and move to Dedicated or go Private from day one. Timeline is pretty tight, regulatory review in Q3 so we want a POC in next 4-6 weeks if possible.
[00:30] Ethan: Great, and to clarify the workloads — Amira can you describe typical prompt sizes and concurrency?
[00:36] Amira: Yeah rough numbers — most prompts are short, 30 to 120 tokens, but we have a tail with 1k+ token context for account summaries. Expected steady-state traffic is about 80 to 150 reqs per second, peak up to 500 rps during workday spikes. Latency target is p50 under 250ms for short prompts and p95 under 900ms for larger context. Also quality threshold: responses must match existing model baseline on intent accuracy > 92%.
[01:02] Priya: ok that helps. A couple follow ups: what's your tolerance for cold-start vs warmed KV cache, and do you need deterministic response ordering for reranking ops?
[01:10] Tom: We can't assume persistent KV cache across pods unless it's within a private deployment; we have strict egress controls so peering and IP allowlists are required. Also encryption in transit is mandatory, and KMS for at-rest.
[01:22] Maya: Noted. Let's walk through the three modes — Hosted, Dedicated, Private — and tradeoffs.
[01:28] Ethan: Hosted gives fastest time-to-value: we can onboard in days, Redwood API, model catalog, streaming responses, and built-in autoscale. The downside is higher per-token cost at our volume and it's tenancy-shared, though we offer SOC2 and data retention controls. Hosted can do burst to handle 500 rps but you'd pay for burst pricing.
[01:45] Luis: Do you have VPC peering for Hosted? Our security team will ask.
[01:50] Priya: For Hosted we offer private endpoints and VPC peering in some regions, but there are restrictions — it's not full private control plane. For strict network isolation and customer-managed KMS you likely need Dedicated or Private.
[02:02] Amira: Dedicated vs Private — what's the difference in practice?
[02:06] Ethan: Dedicated (we sometimes say Redwood Dedicated) is reserved GPU pools for just your org in our infra, with configurable autoscaling policies. You get better unit cost vs Hosted, predictable throughput, and some isolation, but control plane is still managed by Redwood. Private means customer can run our control plane in a VPC or on-prem, customer-managed networking and KMS/HSM — highest isolation and compliance but longer setup and ops burden.
[02:29] Sara: Ops burden meaning our infra team needs to manage nodes?
[02:32] Ethan: For Private on-prem, yes you manage underlying hardware; for Private VPC we provide an appliance and orchestration but network and KMS are customer-managed. Redwood still provides support and the runtime, but it's more like a license + deployment project.
[02:45] Luis: Ok timeline implications? We have 6 weeks to a POC.
[02:49] Maya: Hosted POC could be live within 1-2 weeks once we have prompts and an API key — benchmarks in 48 hours. Dedicated requires provisioning capacity — usually 2-4 weeks depending on commit and region. Private often 6-12 weeks including security approvals and KMS integration. So given your Q3 regulatory window, Hosted -> Dedicated may be the fastest path.
[03:06] Tom: There are data residency constraints for some EU customers; we might need Private for certain datasets.
[03:10] Priya: We can segment traffic — sensitive flows to Private/Dedicated and the rest on Hosted via routing policies. Redwood supports smart routing and fallback to keep services online.
[03:21] Amira: Benchmarks — how do you propose we evaluate? What metrics do you run?
[03:25] Ethan: We'll run a two-phase benchmark: synthetic throughput runs to validate concurrency and p95 latency, then a mixed workload using your real prompt set to validate model quality, per-token cost, and cache hit rates. Key metrics: p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, cost per 1M tokens, cache hit ratio, and model output regression against your baseline. We'll also instrument tracing and token-level cost breakdowns in Redwood Console.
[03:46] Luis: What about quantized model variants — can you run the same eval across float16 vs int8 for cost delta?
[03:52] Priya: Yes, we'll test quantized variants. Note quality can drop on some prompts; we'll tie quality regressions to prompt sets. Redwood Optimize recommends quantization profiles by workload.
[04:03] Sara: For SLA — what uptime and latency SLOs do you guarantee for Dedicated?
[04:07] Maya: We have SLA-backed uptime for Dedicated and priority support. Typical latency guarantees are at the config level — we can commit to p95 under X for specific capacity profiles in contract. Exact SLOs depend on the reserved capacity and model choice.
[04:20] Tom: Security checklist — SOC2 Type II, ISO? What do you provide?
[04:25] Ethan: We have SOC2 Type II, ISO 27001 — I'll attach the security pack. For Private we support customer-managed KMS/HSM and full audit logs, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and retained audit trails. For Hosted we provide encryption at rest and in transit plus customer scoping for data retention.
[04:40] Amira: A practical question: if we start on Hosted and later move to Dedicated, do we need to change prompts or model versions?
[04:45] Priya: No, the API and model versioning are consistent across modes. You can pin model versions and rollout policies independent of infra. We do recommend re-running benchmarks after migration to tune batching and KV cache settings.
[04:58] Luis: Cost sensitivity — we're trying to estimate month-to-month. Can you give a rough delta between Hosted and Dedicated at our volume?
[05:04] Maya: Ballpark: Dedicated can be 30-45% cheaper at sustained high volumes due to reserved GPU pools and better batching, but requires a commit. Hosted is flexible but higher unit cost for sustained traffic. We'll send a detailed pricing sheet with examples.
[05:16] Tom: For the POC bench, we need to mimic peak spikes. Do you support traffic shaping to reproduce burst?
[05:21] Ethan: Yes our bench harness can replay histograms and create synthetic spikes. We'll run both steady-state and spike scenarios. We'll also validate autoscale and fallback behavior, e.g., route to a cheaper model variant if under pressure.
[05:32] Amira: Quality gates — we need confidence that answers don't leak or hallucinate with account summaries. How do you do evals?
[05:37] Priya: We run eval suites against curated prompt sets and compare against baselines. We can run specific tests for hallucination and PII redaction. We'll set up monitors to alert on regression thresholds.
[05:47] Sara: Decision criteria — what would you recommend for us given our constraints?
[05:50] Ethan: Given you have high volume and strict security but a short POC timeline, a phased approach: 1) Hosted POC with VPC endpoints and strict retention to validate quality and latency quickly; 2) Parallel Dedicated sizing exercise and pricing review; 3) If required by residency/KMS, move sensitive flows to Private later. That gives you a fast start and path to lower cost and more isolation.
[06:10] Luis: Sounds reasonable. Any gotchas?
[06:12] Maya: A few: network egress and peering time, KMS integration can take extra cycles, and custom quantization tuning may need extra eval iterations. Also model warm-up and keyset cache priming can affect early latencies.
[06:24] Tom: On priming — can you warm KV cache for known user sessions?
[06:27] Priya: Yes we support prefix and KV caching; for Dedicated/Private you have more control over cache persistence. Hosted caches are managed but you can configure TTLs.
[06:36] Amira: For the benchmark run — what do you need from us?
[06:38] Ethan: Sample prompt set, traffic histogram (timestamps + rps), a couple of representative long-context examples, success criteria (latency & quality), and security POC contacts. We'll do a 2-hour smoke then a 6-hour mixed run for more stability data.
[06:53] Luis: Ok we'll assemble that. Any immediate blockers?
[06:56] Maya: Not really. We'll need your security contact for the questionnaire and a list of endpoints that need residency.
[06:59] Sara: I'll own the security contact and distribution.
[07:03] Ethan: Another thing — fallback policies: if Dedicated is overloaded we can route to a smaller cheaper model variant in Hosted to keep latencies down. We can simulate that in the bench.
[07:12] Amira: For model variants, can you run the same weights quantized and unquantized side-by-side?
[07:16] Priya: Yes, we'll add that to the bench matrix.
[07:20] Luis: For reporting, we need token-level cost breakdown and per-route dashboards.
[07:24] Maya: Redwood Console provides token-level cost and per-model dashboards, traces, and errors. We'll give demo access during the POC.
[07:31] Tom: On networking, we'll need to know required firewall rules for VPC peering and IP ranges.
[07:36] Priya: We'll send a network requirements doc and a template for firewall rules.
[07:40] Maya: Ok let's recap next steps quickly.
[07:43] Maya: 1) Amira to share prompt set + traffic histogram by 3/28. 2) Tom to share network and egress constraints by 3/29. 3) Maya to send pricing + contract templates by 3/27. 4) Ethan to schedule benchmark for week of 3/31 and prepare harness. 5) Redwood to send SOC2 + security pack.
[08:01] Luis: Good. Anything else?
[08:03] Sara: Can we get a sample SSO flow for admin provisioning?
[08:06] Priya: Yes we'll include SAML examples and RBAC roles in the security pack.
[08:10] Maya: Great. We'll follow up with calendar invite for the bench and a 30-minute pre-bench sync to align metrics.
[08:16] Luis: Thanks everyone. Looking forward.
[08:18] Maya: Thanks all. End.
